strengths: First systematic adaptation of Native Sparse Attention (NSA) to video-language models, with a sensible hybrid design (sparse for video tokens, dense GQA for text tokens) that is well-motivated by the redundancy structure of video.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three task domains (long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, spatial reasoning) against a fairly complete set of token-compression and training-free sparse-attention baselines, generally showing competitive or best results.

Extensive and genuinely informative analysis section (6 findings) covering context-length scaling to 128K, optimal global/local attention budget allocation, branch-wise gating dynamics across layers/heads, latency bottleneck attribution, and — most novel — a detailed study of how the three NSA branches differently induce/avoid attention sinks compared to dense attention.
The finding that sparse-trained QKV weights transfer beneficial inductive biases even under dense-attention inference is a nice additional insight beyond the primary efficiency claim.
Large and detailed appendix with subtask-level breakdowns, hyperparameters, and branch-ablation tables that supports reproducibility of the empirical claims.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is limited: the method is largely a direct application of the existing NSA mechanism (Yuan et al., 2025b) to video tokens with a modality-split hybrid attention, rather than a new sparse-attention algorithm; the 'attention as GNN message passing' framing in Sec 2.2 is more rhetorical than a rigorous new contribution.

Performance gains over strong training-free sparse baselines (XAttention, MInference) are often marginal or mixed (e.g., TimeScope 83.7 vs 83.1/82.7; VSIBench 36.1 is not the best among sparse methods, XAttention scores 36.6), undercutting the strength of the central claim of consistent superiority.
Only a single backbone/model size (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) is evaluated; no validation at larger scale or with a different base VLM, limiting evidence for generality of the approach.
Project page/code/model links are blank in the submission, and despite a reproducibility statement, key artifacts (trained model, code) are not actually verifiable at review time.

Minor numeric inconsistencies across tables for the same metric (e.g., VideoNSA LongVideoBench score reported as 60.0 in Table 1, 59.4 in Table 3, and 60.2 in Table 7) raise concerns about experimental bookkeeping/consistency.

The fine-tuned dense baseline (Dense-SFT) underperforms the base model on several benchmarks, suggesting the 216K training set itself is of limited quality, which complicates attributing gains specifically to the sparse-attention mechanism versus training data effects.

While latency of branches is analyzed, there is no direct wall-clock/memory comparison of VideoNSA against the token-compression and training-free sparse baselines in the main results table, making the practical efficiency argument less concrete than the accuracy claims.

Many of the 'findings' are descriptive empirical observations without deeper mechanistic explanation or actionable design guidance beyond the specific trained model, somewhat limiting broader significance for the community.

strengths: The paper conducts an unusually thorough empirical investigation, including branch-combination ablations, context-length scaling to 128K, attention-budget scaling, gating/inter-head similarity analysis, attention-sink characterization, and efficiency (FLOPs/latency) breakdowns, which together provide useful practical insights for the community even beyond the core method.

VideoNSA is evaluated against a reasonably broad set of baselines (token compression: FastV, VScan, VisionZip; training-free sparse attention: Tri-Shape, MInference, FlexPrefill, XAttention; quantization: AWQ) across three task categories (long-video, temporal reasoning, spatial understanding) plus two additional benchmarks in the appendix (LSDBench, VideoEvalPro), showing generally competitive or best results.

The hybrid design (dense attention for text, NSA for vision) is a sensible, well-motivated architectural choice that preserves instruction-following while enabling scalable sparse attention on the dominant vision token stream.

The attention-sink analysis (Finding 6) and the gating-branch specialization analysis (Finding 3/4) are interesting and provide mechanistic insight into why/how sparse attention behaves differently in video versus text contexts, supported by additional appendix comparisons against text-only NSA.
Reasonably strong reproducibility effort: detailed training hyperparameters, evaluation settings, and dataset construction are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a fairly direct adaptation of an existing method (NSA, Yuan et al. 2025c) to video by setting block size equal to per-frame token count and applying a hybrid dense/sparse split by modality; the architectural novelty beyond this straightforward adaptation is limited.

Reported gains over strong training-free sparse-attention baselines (XAttention, MInference) are often marginal or mixed (e.g., Table 1: VideoNSA 60.0 vs XAttention 59.1 on LVB, 83.7 vs 83.1 on TimeScope, 36.1 vs 36.6 on VSIBench where VideoNSA is actually slightly worse), making the practical significance of the proposed method less clear despite requiring substantial additional training (4600 H100 hours) that the baselines do not.

Table 3 shows that transferring the learned sparse-trained weights to dense attention (Dense-NSA) sometimes matches or nearly matches full VideoNSA performance, raising questions about how much of the improvement stems from the sparse architecture itself versus the training data/recipe used to fine-tune the backbone.

The efficiency story is weaker in practice than in theory: theoretical FLOPs suggest 0.24x cost relative to dense attention, but the actual implementation only achieves 0.56x FLOPs and modest real-world speedups (per Appendix Q/Figure 26) due to kernel padding constraints from the unusual Qwen2.5-VL GQA head configuration, undermining the "hardware-aware" efficiency claims made in the abstract/intro.
Only a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and single model scale is evaluated; no experiments at larger scale or with alternative backbones are provided to test generality of the approach.

The paper packs in six distinct "findings" plus extensive appendices, which, while thorough, dilutes focus and depth of analysis for any single finding; several analyses (e.g., routing-path stability theory in Appendix M) are somewhat speculative/post-hoc justifications rather than rigorously validated claims.

Comparisons with training-free baselines are not entirely apples-to-apples, since VideoNSA benefits from end-to-end fine-tuning on 216K video QA pairs that the baselines do not receive; the Dense-SFT ablation partially addresses this but a more controlled comparison (e.g., fine-tuning baselines with the same data under their sparse settings) would strengthen the claims.
